summary: The note is a Wikipedia article on ironic process theory, which holds that deliberately trying to avoid a thought or emotion paradoxically makes it occur more often and more intensely. It traces the theory to Daniel Wegner's 1987 white bear experiments, explains his two-process mechanism (operating and monitoring processes), and reviews supporting evidence on restrained eating and anger suppression. It also covers applications in mood disorders and memory, counteracting strategies, criticism, earlier literary and cultural references, and the alternative psychological reactance explanation.
one_line: Ironic process theory holds that intentionally suppressing a thought makes it recur more frequently, a effect first studied by Daniel Wegner in 1987.
key_facts: Ironic process theory (IPT) suggests that attempting to avoid a thought or feeling a certain emotion produces a paradoxical effect in which the thought or emotion occurs more frequently and more intensely.
IPT is also known as "ironic rebound" or "the white bear problem."
Social psychologist Daniel Wegner first studied ironic process theory in a laboratory setting in 1987.
Wegner's first 1987 experiment involved 34 participants who were randomly allocated to initial suppression or initial expression conditions.
In Wegner's second experiment, a third group thought of a red Volkswagen as a distractor during the suppression task, and this group rang the bell less frequently.

Wegner's model holds that successful thought suppression requires two simultaneous processes: an operating process that occupies mental resources to will away the thought, and a monitoring process that searches for unwanted thoughts and shifts attention to other objects.
Boon et al. conducted an experiment in 2002 on ice-cream consumption, in which restrained participants ate more than unrestrained participants, and ate even more when distracted.
Burns et al. conducted a 2008 experiment on chronic low back pain patients, finding that the suppression group reported greater anger and pain intensity and showed more pain behaviours.
The theory can be applied in treating mood disorders such as anxiety and depression, and therapists are advised to encourage patients to accept negative feelings rather than suppress them.
Wegner's study used a white bear, and later studies in this area used only one stimulus, so generalisability of the theory is still in question.

In Winter Notes on Summer Impressions (1863), Fyodor Dostoevsky wrote: "Try to pose for yourself this task: not to think of a polar bear, and you will see that the cursed thing will come to mind every minute."
Psychological reactance theory is an alternative explanation in which threatened autonomy produces reactive thoughts, causing participants to think of the white bear even more.
A research team at Ohio State University used clickers with 283 college students and found men averaged 19 thoughts about sex per day while women thought about sex ten times per day.

Wegner and others identified counteractive strategies including focusing on a distractor, postponing the thought, decreasing mental load by cutting back on multitasking, consciously exposing oneself to the thought, and practicing meditation and mindfulness.
The 1984 movie Ghostbusters and the Black Mirror episode "White Bear" both feature the idea, and the mind game "The Game" is based on it.
